title: Multiple Assignment
summary: Declare and assign several variables in one line, swap and rotate values without a temporary variable, and group declarations in var blocks.
intro: Go lets you put several names on the left of `=` or `:=` and several values on the right. That makes related declarations shorter and turns swaps into one line.

steps.title: Several at once
steps.body:
List the names on the left and the values on the right, separated by commas. Values pair up by position, so the counts must match.

```go
a, b := 1, 2
var x, y int = 10, 20
n, s := 5, "five"
fmt.Println(a, b, x, y, n, s) // 1 2 10 20 5 five
```

With `:=` each variable gets the type of its own value, so one line can mix an `int` and a `string`. With `var x, y int = ...` every name shares the one type you wrote. Here `int` is optional because `10` and `20` default to `int` anyway, but the form matters when you want a different type, such as `float64`.

To declare a group of related variables, use a `var ( ... )` block, the same shape as the `const` block you already know. gofmt lines up the `=` signs.

```go harness
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	{{code}}
	fmt.Println(name, ready)
}
```

```go
var (
	name  = "Ada"
	ready = true
)
```

Every variable still has to be used, or the program will not compile.

example.title: Game window settings
example.prompt: Declare the settings of a game window three different ways, then print them all on one line.
example.explanation: The `var` block declares `title` as a `string` and `fullscreen` as a `bool`, inferred from their values. The next line gives `width` and `height` the type `int` together. Then `:=` declares `player` as a `string` and `lives` as an `int` in one go. `fmt.Println` joins all six values with spaces.

practice.title: Recipe card
practice.prompt:
Declare a recipe with multiple declarations and print it on one line.

1. In a `var ( ... )` block, declare `dish` as `"pancakes"` and `vegan` as `true`.
2. On one line, declare `servings` as `4` and `minutes` as `20` with `var` and the type `int`.
3. On one line, declare `chef` as `"Sam"` and `rating` as `4.5` with `:=`.
4. Print all six values in that order with one `fmt.Println`.

Expected output:

```text
pancakes true 4 20 Sam 4.5
```
hints: Copy the shape of the game window example and change the names and values.
`rating` becomes a `float64` because `4.5` has a decimal point. `chef, rating := "Sam", 4.5` is fine even though the types differ.

steps.title: Swap and rotate
steps.body:
Plain `=` works with several names too, and it gives you a swap in one line:

```go harness
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	a, b := 1, 2
	{{code}}
	fmt.Println(a, b)
}
```

```go
a, b = b, a
```

This works because Go evaluates the whole right side first, then assigns. It reads `b` and `a`, holds both values, and only then writes them into `a` and `b`. Two separate lines would break:

```go harness
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	a, b := 1, 2
	{{code}}
	fmt.Println(a, b)
}
```

```go
a = b // the old a is gone
b = a // b gets its own value back
```

The same rule rotates three values with no temporary variable. Each name on the left receives the value of the name in the same position on the right:

```go harness
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	a, b, c := 1, 2, 3
	{{code}}
}
```

```go
a, b, c = b, c, a    // rotate left
fmt.Println(a, b, c) // 2 3 1
a, b, c = c, a, b    // rotate right
fmt.Println(a, b, c) // 1 2 3
```

In memory each variable keeps its own slot. The swap copies values between the slots, and for strings that copy is cheap: Go copies a small header that points at the text, not the text itself. The variables must already exist and the types must fit, since `=` never declares anything.

example.title: Race results
example.prompt: Swap two names, then rotate three runners one place right, printing before and after each change.
example.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	first, second := "Ana", "Ben"
	fmt.Println(first, second)
	first, second = second, first
	fmt.Println(first, second)

	gold, silver, bronze := "Kim", "Lou", "Max"
	fmt.Println(gold, silver, bronze)
	// Rotate one place right: the last runner moves to the front
	gold, silver, bronze = bronze, gold, silver
	fmt.Println(gold, silver, bronze)
}
example.output:
Ana Ben
Ben Ana
Kim Lou Max
Max Kim Lou
example.explanation: `first, second = second, first` reads `"Ben"` and `"Ana"` before writing either variable, so nothing is lost. For the rotation the right side reads `Max Kim Lou`, then `gold`, `silver` and `bronze` take those values in order, so every runner moves one place right and the last one wraps to the front.

practice.title: Swap numbers, rotate colors
practice.prompt:
Swap two numbers and rotate three colors one place left, each with a single assignment.

1. Swap `x` and `y` with one assignment, between the two prints that are already there.
2. Rotate `left`, `middle` and `right` one place left with one assignment, so the first color moves to the end.
3. Keep the four `fmt.Println` lines so the values print before and after each change.

Expected output:

```text
3 8
8 3
red green blue
green blue red
```
practice.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	x, y := 3, 8
	fmt.Println(x, y)
	x, y = y, x
	fmt.Println(x, y)

	left, middle, right := "red", "green", "blue"
	fmt.Println(left, middle, right)
	// Rotate one place left: the first color moves to the end
	left, middle, right = middle, right, left
	fmt.Println(left, middle, right)
}

tests.output:
3 8
8 3
red green blue
green blue red

hints: A swap is `x, y = y, x`. Use `=`, not `:=`, because both variables already exist.
After the rotation `left` should hold the old `middle`, `middle` the old `right`, and `right` the old `left`.

steps.title: Redeclaring with :=
steps.body:
`:=` declares variables, so it needs at least one new name on its left. If every name already exists in the same scope, the compiler stops you:

```go error
x, y := 1, 2
x, y := 3, 4 // error: no new variables on left side of :=
```

Use `=` for that. When at least one name is new, `:=` is allowed, and the names that already exist in the same scope are simply assigned, not declared again:

```go
x, y := 1, 2
y, z := 30, 40       // z is new, y is assigned 30
fmt.Println(x, y, z) // 1 30 40
```

Since `y` is the same variable, its type cannot change: assigning a string to it here would fail. The blank identifier `_` never counts as new, so `_, x := 5, 6` fails when `x` already exists. Later you will lean on this rule to write `v, err :=` several times in a row with the same `err`.

One catch: the rule only applies within the same scope. Inside an inner block, `:=` makes a brand new variable that hides the outer one. A later lesson shows that.

example.title: Reusing a name
example.prompt: Declare two variables, then use := again with one old name and one new name.
example.explanation: The first `:=` declares `x` and `y`. The second `:=` is legal because `z` is new. `y` already exists in the same scope, so it is reassigned to `30` instead of being declared again, and `x` is untouched.

practice.title: Fruit basket
practice.prompt:
Update one fruit count and add a new fruit with a single :=.

1. Below the first print, write one `:=` that sets `pears` to `8` and declares `plums` as `6`.
2. Change the last `fmt.Println` to print `apples`, `pears` and `plums`.

Expected output:

```text
5 3
5 8 6
```
practice.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	apples, pears := 5, 3
	fmt.Println(apples, pears)
	pears, plums := 8, 6
	fmt.Println(apples, pears, plums)
}
hints: Put the existing name and the new name together on the left: `pears, plums := ...`.
Plain `=` would not work here, because `plums` does not exist yet. The new name is what makes `:=` legal.

recap:
- `a, b := 1, 2` declares several variables at once, and each gets the type of its own value.
- `var x, y int = 10, 20` gives every name the same type.
- A `var ( ... )` block groups related declarations.
- The whole right side is evaluated before anything is assigned, so `a, b = b, a` swaps and `a, b, c = b, c, a` rotates.
- `:=` needs at least one new name on the left. Names that already exist in the same scope are just assigned.
